question: Both my sister (1) / and me (2) / went to a boarding school. (3) / No error (4).
explanation: Correction shown in the class: “Both my sister and I went to a boarding school.”

question: My uncle forced (1) / my friend and I (2) / to stay back. (3) / No error (4).
explanation: After “forced”, the pronoun is an object; the class uses “my friend and me”.

question: He invited (1) / my sister and I (2) / to the party. (3) / No error (4).
explanation: The pronoun is the object of “invited”; use “my sister and me”.

question: This gift is for you and ___.
explanation: After the preposition “for”, use the objective pronoun “me”.

question: You and ___ are responsible for the project.
explanation: The pronoun is part of the subject “You and I”.

question: Between you and I (1) / there is no misunderstanding. (2) / We are clear about it. (3) / No error (4).
explanation: After “between”, use the objective form: “between you and me”.

question: Everyone except he (1) / is aware of the plan. (2) / You should inform him. (3) / No error (4).
explanation: After “except”, use the objective pronoun “him”.

question: There was a (1) / comparison between (2) / you and he (3) / no error (4).
explanation: After “between”, both pronouns should be objective: “between you and him”.

question: Unless two or more members object to him joining the club, we shall have to accept his application for membership.
explanation: The slide highlights “him joining” after “object to”.

question: I was surprised and pleased when I was informed of me winning the contest.
explanation: The slide correction uses the possessive form before the gerund: “of my winning the contest”.

question: My teacher did not object to me using the calculator.
explanation: The slide focuses on the pronoun used with the -ing form after “object to”.

question: He, you and I are going to play Cricket.
explanation: The class teaches the preferred sequence as 2 + 3 + 1: You + third person + I.

question: I and you are going to watch movie.
explanation: The class applies the preferred sequence and gives “You and I” as the natural order.

question: Jai, I and Shivam have finished our work.
explanation: The class rearranges the subject according to the taught sequence and uses “our” for the group containing I.

question: He and you are found guilty.
explanation: The class applies the 2 + 3 + 1 order: “You and he …”.

question: She and you are at fault and will be punished.
explanation: The class applies the 2 + 3 + 1 order: “You and she …”.

question: You and they are responsible.
explanation: The slide marks this compound-subject sentence as correct.

question: You and he made a mistake.
explanation: The slide marks this compound-subject sentence as correct.

question: You and he will win the match.
explanation: The slide marks this compound-subject sentence as correct.

question: You and they have done a great job.
explanation: The slide marks this compound-subject sentence as correct.

question: John, I and Hari (1) / have finished (2) / our studies. (3) / No error (4).
explanation: The class rearranges the subject to “John, Hari and I”.

question: I and he (1) / have prepared (2) / the lesson thoroughly. (3) / No error. (4)
explanation: The preferred order taught is “He and I”.

question: You and he have done our/their/his/her work.
explanation: The class note tests possessive agreement after a compound subject.

question: You, he and I have done our/your/their/my/his job.
explanation: The class note highlights “our” when referring to the whole group containing You, he and I.

question: The climate of Shimla is colder than Delhi.
explanation: The class highlights comparison of comparable entities, i.e. Shimla’s climate with Delhi’s climate.

question: The questions in this book are easier than that book.
explanation: The class highlights comparing like things: questions with questions, not questions with a book.

question: Your job is better than Ram’s.
explanation: “Ram’s” represents “Ram’s job” in the comparison.

question: His voice is sweeter than you.
explanation: The class correction uses the possessive pronoun: “His voice is sweeter than yours.”

question: The problems in India are similar to China.
explanation: The class highlights comparison of like entities: India’s problems with China’s problems.

question: The phone that (1) / my father bought was different (2) / from yours. (3) / No error (4).
explanation: The slide marks “from yours” as correct; “yours” stands for “your phone”.

question: Her handwriting (1) / is definitely more (2) / beautiful than me. (3) / No Error (4)
explanation: The class correction uses “mine”: compare her handwriting with my handwriting.

question: He is (1) / fatter (2) / than me. (3) / No error (4)
explanation: The slide marks this sentence as having no error in the pattern shown.
